name: Georgian
intro: Learn Mkhedruli: ქართული. Georgian has ejective consonants contrasting with aspirated and voiced series; audio and articulation practice are essential. It does not have grammatical gender or articles like German. Verb morphology is highly structured and requires long-term pattern learning. This volume gives a map and controlled examples, not a promise that a few suffix rules generate every verb.

foundation.name: Georgian
notes: Mkhedruli is the ordinary modern script, written left to right. Mtavruli forms are used for display capitals. Older scripts are outside the beginner writing inventory. Start by copying each letter, then reading it in a word.

Several stops and affricates distinguish voiced, aspirated and ejective sounds. Romanisation uses an apostrophe for ejectives here: k’, p’, t’, ts’, ch’, q’. The apostrophe is a pronunciation marker, not a separate Georgian letter.

Consonant clusters can be long. Break them into articulatory movements, then join them slowly; avoid inserting an English or Hindi vowel between every consonant. Georgian vowels are a/e/i/o/u. Stress is comparatively weak and should be learned from phrases.
building: სახლი → სახლში = house → in the house. Recognise the stem and the attached relation marker.

ბავშვი კითხულობს წიგნს. = The child reads a book. ბავშვმა წაიკითხა წიგნი. = The child read the book. A tense/aspect series can change the case alignment; do not transfer the first pattern mechanically to the second.
ვისწავლი = I will learn; ვსწავლობ = I study / am studying. Georgian verbs carry information about participants and screeves; learn forms in a sentence with their noun cases.

sections.title: Script, sound and case relationships
sections.explanation: Mkhedruli has 33 letters in the modern alphabet. Learn ejectives such as კ, პ and ტ separately from aspirated ქ, ფ and თ. Consonant clusters should be practised in meaningful words rather than by inserting English vowels. Georgian cases include nominative, ergative, dative, genitive, instrumental, adverbial and vocative. Their use in subject/object relationships depends partly on verb class and screeve.
examples: A local relation expressed with -ში; exact direction is supplied by the predicate/context.
exercises: Why is a one-case-per-English-role chart insufficient?
Subject and object marking can change with verb class and tense/aspect/mood series.
How should ejectives be learned?
With a reliable acoustic/articulatory model and contrasts, not by treating an apostrophe in romanisation as a sound.

sections.title: Verb classes, screeves and argument marking
sections.explanation: A screeve is a coordinated set of tense/aspect/mood forms, not just an English tense label. Georgian verbs can index multiple participants. In many transitive patterns, nominative subject in one series contrasts with ergative subject in the aorist series; other verb classes differ. Learn a verb with its principal patterns, arguments and model sentences. Avoid extending a single transitive paradigm to all verbs.
examples: A bounded past reading construction; forms should be learned as a pattern.
exercises: What should a Georgian verb note contain?
Class, core forms, participant marking, case patterns and verified examples.
Why is a screeve not identical to an English tense?
It packages multiple grammatical dimensions and interacts with argument marking.

sections.title: Possession, clauses and questions
sections.explanation: Possession and experiencer constructions can differ from English subject-verb patterns. Postpositions and case express relationships. რომ introduces many complement structures; relative and interrogative constructions require attention to clause roles. Word order is flexible but constrained by information structure and emphasis. Flexibility does not mean all orders are pragmatically equivalent.
examples: I think that this is correct.
exercises: What must a translation preserve beyond word meanings?
Participant relations, case, verb morphology, information structure and register.
Identify the connector in the second example.
რომ introduces the proposition represented as the thought content.

sections.title: Professional requests and uncertainty
sections.explanation: Professional language needs precise reference and respectful requests, not a memorised greeting alone. Learn fixed courteous phrases and then vary their objects. შესაძლებელია presents possibility; საჭიროა necessity. Confirm nuanced verb forms with a modern grammar, dictionary or competent speaker. In this language especially, extensive input and feedback matter for reliable production.
exercises: Ask a professional to clarify rather than guessing a technical term.
შეგიძლიათ ეს განმარტოთ? Add the exact term or quotation as the context.
Why keep a verified sentence bank?
Complex morphology makes an attested pattern more useful than an invented suffix combination.

sections.title: Professional reading and analysis
sections.explanation:
Teaching passage: ეს შედეგი მნიშვნელოვანია, მაგრამ დამატებითი კვლევა საჭიროა. მონაცემები უნდა შევამოწმოთ. დასკვნა ჯერ საბოლოო არ არის.
Translation: This result is important, but additional research is needed. We must check the data. The conclusion is not yet final. The passage uses a contrast and an explicit limitation; it is a controlled teaching example, not a real research report.
examples: The conclusion is not yet final.
ჯერ and negation preserve provisional status.
Necessity construction with a first-person plural action.
exercises: Summarise the practical recommendation.
Check the data and obtain further research before treating the conclusion as final.
Annotate an authentic Georgian page.
Identify predicates, arguments, cases, unknown terms and one clear limitation before producing a paraphrase.

rules.title: Independent pronouns
rules.explanation: Pronouns identify participants; verbs often also encode participants, allowing omission. Is can refer to he/she/it without English grammatical gender. Georgian verb classes use distinct case alignments.

examples.translation: I work in a pharmacy.
I am tired and I want to go to bed.

examples.native: მე ვფიქრობ, რომ მე ვარ მთვრალი.
examples.translation: I think I'm drunk.

rules.title: Present copula
rules.explanation: Copula forms distinguish person and number: ვარ, ხარ, არის, ვართ, ხართ, არიან. Short/attached realisations occur in discourse. Learn a complete predicate rather than replacing every English be identically.

examples.translation: These are students.

examples.native: არის ტომი უფრო უფროსი ვიდრე შენ?
examples.translation: Is Tom older than you?
They are both good teachers.

rules.title: Negation
rules.explanation: არ commonly negates; ვერ commonly expresses inability/failure to perform. Their interpretations interact with the verb and context. They are not interchangeable merely because both create a negative meaning.

examples.native: უბრალოდ არ ვიცი რა უნდა ვთქვა.
examples.translation: I just don't know what to say.

examples.native: მე დავიფიცე, რომ არასოდეს აღარ დაველაპარაკები.
examples.translation: I vowed that I would never speak to her again.
I don't live in this city.

rules.title: Demonstratives
rules.explanation: Demonstrative forms change with case and construction. Es often points to this; is to that or a previously mentioned referent. The following noun’s relation determines an inflected form.

examples.native: გელამ თქვა, რომ მამა წავიდა ქალაქში.
examples.translation: Gela said that Father went into the city.

examples.native: ჩვეს სკოლას ჯამში აქვს ოცდაოთხი კლასი.
examples.translation: Our school has twenty-four classes in all.
Labor created man.

rules.title: Possessive pronouns
rules.explanation: Possessive forms modify a noun and themselves inflect in relevant contexts. Learn the complete phrase. Possession predicates use particular verbal classes and participant marking.

examples.translation: Our meeting was quite accidental.
Here is your key.
Here is your dog.

rules.title: Questions: people and things
rules.explanation: Question words inflect for role and case. ვინ asks who; რა asks what, with forms such as რას for an appropriate oblique/object role. Case depends on the verb series and construction.

examples.translation: I'm cold. May I close the window?
The new store is going to open next week.
Who gave you permission?

rules.title: Questions: place and manner
rules.explanation: Different question forms request location, source, direction, manner, time or reason. The English word where can hide distinctions. Preserve the relation in your answer.

examples.translation: Where do you want to go?
That is what they study English for.
How can I be sure?

rules.title: Plural forms
rules.explanation: Many nouns form a plural with -ები, sometimes with stem changes. Other number/case combinations need their own endings. Quantified phrases do not mechanically follow English plural usage.

examples.translation: Mary loves horses.

examples.native: სახლში თუ დამაგვიანდება წასვლა, ნუ დამელოდები.
examples.translation: If I should be late getting home, please don't wait up for me.
Close your eyes, and count to ten.

rules.title: Inside/location -ში
rules.explanation: Attached -ში expresses many in/into relations. The verb and context distinguish position from movement; the suffix does not encode the full English prepositional phrase by itself.

examples.translation: Can I visit Australia with Tom?

examples.native: საშას ქონდა ძლიერი ტკივილი მარჯვენა ხელში.
examples.translation: Sasha had a sharp pain in her right hand.
I want to go to Tokyo.

rules.title: Source -დან
rules.explanation: Attached -დან expresses many from/source relations, with stem and linking changes. Learn a word’s actual inflection rather than cutting any final syllable off and adding the suffix.

examples.translation: I am from Russia.
I am from Norway.
I come from America.

rules.title: Possessor and relation forms
rules.explanation: Genitive -ის and its stem changes express possession and support other relations. The governing postposition or noun phrase determines the case, not English word order alone.

examples.translation: The skyscraper is in the center of the city.
He's the man of the house.
I'll write a book.

rules.title: Possession predicates
rules.explanation: Possession predicates encode participants in a class-specific way. English I have is not a reliable model for the noun cases. Learn the possessor and possessed item together with each form.

examples.translation: I have a green shirt.
I have a lot to do.
I have a big house.

rules.title: Want predicates
rules.explanation: Want predicates have their own experiencer/participant pattern. უნდა also occurs in necessity constructions. Use the complement and context to distinguish desire from should/must meanings.

examples.translation: I want to talk to you.
I want to be an actress.
Which book do you want?

rules.title: Common present verbs
rules.explanation: Georgian verbs may encode multiple participants. The present-series noun cases depend on verb class. Memorise a meaningful sentence and compare a small paradigm rather than guessing from one prefix.

examples.native: მხოლოდ ვიცი ზოგიერთი სიტყვა და ფრაზა.
examples.translation: I only know some words and phrases.
I don't speak Japanese.
I think Tom will make breakfast.

rules.title: Past-series verbs
rules.explanation: Past forms belong to different screeves and verb classes. Some active verbs change subject/object case marking in the aorist series. There is no single past ending that can be applied to every Georgian verb.

examples.translation: No more than 50 people came.

examples.native: მარი ერთ-ერათი ყველაზე პოპულარული გოგო იყო.
examples.translation: Mary was not one of the most popular girls.
Mary was in heaven.

rules.title: Future-series forms
rules.explanation: Future forms may involve a preverb and a class-specific stem. Future morphology and argument marking must be learned together. A preverb can also contribute lexical direction or meaning.

examples.translation: He will go to the dentist.
He will be very nice.

rules.title: Content and relative linking
rules.explanation: რომ links many content and dependent clauses. Its English translation depends on the construction, and the dependent verb form may reflect the speaker’s attitude or the governing predicate.

examples.translation: He says that he knows you.

examples.native: ჩვენ შევთანხმდით, რომ სამსახურში თავს შევიკავებდით მოწევისაგან.
examples.translation: We agreed to refrain from smoking while we are at work.
I want Nino to win.

rules.title: Conditions
rules.explanation: თუ introduces many if/whether contexts. Verb screeve and surrounding discourse determine the temporal/hypothetical relation. Do not treat the connector alone as a full conditional rule.

examples.translation: If you hurry, you will overtake him.
Are you a man or a woman?

examples.native: კომპიუტერს თუ გამოიყენებ ინფორმაციის შენახვას შეძლებ.
examples.translation: If you use a computer, you can retain information.

rules.title: Coordination and contrast
rules.explanation: და joins, მაგრამ contrasts, and ან gives an alternative. Keep like structures parallel when coordinating. Their meaning does not replace the case and verb rules inside each clause.

examples.native: დილაობით მხოლოდ ტოსტს და ყავას მივირთმევ.
examples.translation: I only have toast and coffee in the morning.
We'll go with you.
This place is very pleasant.

rules.title: Postpositions and stance
rules.explanation: Postpositions select a noun relationship/case; ალბათ marks a probability and შეიძლება possibility in relevant constructions. Professional statements should distinguish factual evidence from a tentative reading.

examples.translation: This is a book about obesity.
This is a book about Georgia.
I'll talk about you.

grammarTerms: Noun
A word naming a person, thing or idea: student, book, freedom.
Verb
A word describing an action or state: read, know, be.
Subject
The participant linked to the main verb’s subject pattern. In The student reads a book, the student is the subject.
Object
A participant selected by a verb. In The student reads a book, a book is the direct object.
Agreement
One word changes to match another, for example an adjective matching a noun’s gender and number.
Case
A noun/pronoun form marking its relationship in a sentence. Cases can mark subjects, objects, possession or relations usually expressed by English prepositions.
Gender
A grammatical noun class. It does not always describe the sex of a person or any physical property.
Tense
A verb system that relates a situation to a time, often past or non-past.
Aspect
How a situation is viewed: unfolding, completed, habitual, experienced or in a resulting state.
Infinitive
A non-finite verb form often used for a dictionary entry or a complement. It does not by itself give the ordinary person/tense pattern.
Participle
A verb-derived form used in compound predicates or as a modifier; its exact function depends on the language and construction.
Clause
A unit organised around a predicate. One sentence can contain several clauses.
Register
Language choices suited to a situation: casual conversation, polite requests, academic writing or another context.
